instruction.essential_question: What must be known before a meter lead touches a circuit?
preparation: Verify every trainer is current-limited to 24 V DC.
Stage one damaged lead set as a clearly labeled inspection example.
materials: CAT-rated digital multimeter with fused current input

activities.description: Sort sample measurement scenarios into proceed, correct first, and stop-work groups.
Trace the decisions from expected quantity and energy state to function, lead ports, and connection method.
State one condition that requires de-energization and one that requires stopping work.

common_technician_errors: Choosing a meter function before identifying the expected quantity.
Treating an undamaged-looking lead as proof that it is suitable.
instruction.instructor_shop_tip: Require learners to say the expected result aloud before they connect the meter.
instruction.flex_activities: Use additional scenario cards for learners who finish early.

instruction.essential_question: Why do voltage and current measurements require different circuit connections?

activities.description: Inspect a meter setup and identify the deliberate configuration error.
Observe and narrate live-dead-live verification, parallel voltage measurement, and series current measurement.
Rehearse function, port, and connection choices on a de-energized trainer.
Sketch the meter connection for one assigned quantity.

common_technician_errors: Changing lead ports while the circuit is energized.
instruction.instructor_shop_tip: Pause before energizing and have the class audit the complete setup.
instruction.flex_activities: Compare autoranging and manual-ranging meter displays.

instruction.essential_question: How does a measured value become trustworthy evidence?

activities.description: Predict the acceptable range for three trainer measurements.
Complete voltage, resistance, and current measurements using the lab procedure.
Defend one tolerance decision using the expected and measured values.

common_technician_errors: Recording a number without its unit.
Comparing a measurement with a nominal value but ignoring tolerance.
instruction.instructor_shop_tip: Check the current-input fuse before diagnosing a learner's zero-current reading.
instruction.flex_activities: Repeat one measurement on a second trainer and compare tolerances.

instruction.essential_question: Can the complete measurement process be performed safely and independently?

activities.description: Individually review the practical rubric and identify the stop-work criteria.
Perform the assigned voltage, resistance, and current measurements without coaching.
Submit the signed measurement record and restore the station.

common_technician_errors: Leaving the lead in the current port.
instruction.instructor_shop_tip: Score the process and safety controls as well as numerical accuracy.
instruction.flex_activities: Use an oral safety briefing while learners wait for a practical station.

instruction.essential_question: Which electrical quantities are shared and which divide in each circuit topology?
preparation: Verify component values on both circuit trainers.
Prepare one worked example and one incomplete schematic.

activities.description: Classify four schematics as series, parallel, or neither.
Calculate expected source, branch, component, and equivalent values from trainer schematics.
Explain which single measurement would best test one assigned prediction.

common_technician_errors: Applying a series rule to parallel branch current.
Calculating after measuring and treating the measurement as the prediction.
instruction.instructor_shop_tip: Keep expected values visible beside measured values so discrepancies drive the next question.
instruction.flex_activities: Calculate the effect of one resistor tolerance at its upper limit.

instruction.essential_question: What should be investigated when a sound calculation and a careful measurement disagree?

activities.description: Audit a sample expected-versus-measured table for missing evidence.
Finalize expected values and identify acceptable tolerances before assembly.
Build both topologies, inspect before energizing, and compare measurements with predictions.
Identify the strongest evidence that each assembled circuit matches its schematic.

common_technician_errors: Moving several conductors before documenting the original discrepancy.
instruction.instructor_shop_tip: Photograph or sketch the circuit before correcting a wiring discrepancy.
instruction.flex_activities: Swap stations and audit another team's evidence table.

instruction.essential_question: How can each test eliminate the largest number of possible fault locations?

activities.description: Order five diagnostic actions from complaint verification through confirmation.
Interpret measurements that distinguish open, short, and high-resistance symptoms.
Observe half-split and loaded voltage-drop demonstrations, then propose each next test.
Write the expected result for the first test on an assigned fault card.

common_technician_errors: Replacing a component because it is easy to reach rather than because evidence implicates it.
Using resistance testing on an energized circuit.
instruction.instructor_shop_tip: Ask what a passing result eliminates before allowing the next measurement.
instruction.flex_activities: Model a second fault using only a schematic and provided readings.

instruction.essential_question: Does the recorded evidence uniquely support the diagnosis?

activities.description: Review the individual practical rubric and diagnostic worksheet.
Verify, isolate, identify, remove, and confirm one instructor-installed trainer fault.
Submit the diagnostic worksheet and explain the confirming measurement.

common_technician_errors: Declaring the fault before one measurement uniquely supports it.
Failing to confirm normal operation after removing the fault.
instruction.instructor_shop_tip: Use equivalent fault cards across stations and record the selected card with the rubric.
instruction.flex_activities: Learners awaiting a station critique a completed diagnostic record.
